L000033	\title{Diverse properties of electron Forbush decreases revealed by the Dark Matter Particle Explorer}
L000034	
L000035	\input{author20250812.tex}
L000036	
L000037	\begin{abstract}
L000038	The Forbush decrease (FD) of cosmic rays is an important probe of the
L000039	interplanetary environment disturbed by solar activities. In this work,
L000040	we study the properties of 8 FDs electrons (including positrons) between
L000041	2 GeV and 20 GeV from January, 2016 to March, 2024, with the Dark Matter
L000042	Particle Explorer. The maximum decrease amplitudes of these events are
L000043	about $30\%-15\%$, and the amplitudes reduce with energy. The recovery
L000044	time of these events shows diverse behaviors of their energy-dependence.
L000045	Some of them show strong energy-dependence, while some have a nearly
L000046	constant recovery time. It has been shown that such diverse behaviors
L000047	could be related with the geometry of the disturbed regions of the
L000048	interplanetary space by coronal mass ejections (CME), represented by the
L000049	combined effect of the CME velocity, angular spread, and ejection direction.
L000050	\end{abstract}
L000051	
L000052	\pacs{96.25.Qr,98.70.Sa}
L000053	
L000054	\maketitle
L000055	
L000056	{\it Introduction.} ---
L000057	Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) are affected by heliospheric plasma and the
L000058	associated magnetic fields when propagating through the solar system,
L000059	resulting in flux variations at different time scales (e.g.,
L000060	\cite{2000SSRv...93...55C,2013LRSP...10....3P}).
L000061	One type of short-time variations, known as Forbush decreases (FDs)
L000062	\cite{1937PhRv...51.1108F,1937Natur.140..316H}, is the quick drop and
L000063	relatively slow recovery of the GCR fluxes over timescales of days to
L000064	weeks. FDs are caused by energetic solar activities such as coronal mass
L000065	ejections (CMEs) \cite{2010SoPh..263..223Y, 2000SSRv...93...55C} or
L000066	corotating interaction regions (CIRs) \cite{1999AdSpR..23..567H},
L000067	which disturb the interplanetary space and block part of GCRs from
L000068	reaching the detector. Fast CMEs can drive strong interplanetary shocks
L000069	that also play an important role in generating FDs, such as the two-step
L000070	FD including an initial decrease by the shock and a further reduction
L000071	when the CME itself arrives \cite{2011JGRA..11611103J}. FDs have also
L000072	been observed far away from the Earth
L000073	\cite{2018A&A...611A..79G,1993JGR....98....1B,2019ApJ...874..167A},
L000074	indicating that they are universal phenomenon in the solar system.
L000075	
L000076	FDs are widely studied by ground-based neutron monitors (NMs) or muon
L000077	detectors (MDs), which measure secondary particles produced by interactions
L000078	between hadronic GCRs and the atmosphere. The NM or MD data show the
L000079	integral variations of the GCR intensities above specific energies,
L000080	which depend on locations of the detectors due to a latitude dependent
L000081	geomagnetic vertical rigidity cutoff (VRC; \cite{2005AdSpR..36.2012S}).
L000082	Nonetheless, direct measurements by space experiments, in spite that
L000083	they are limited by effective areas, provide better composition and
L000084	energy resolution, and are thus crucial to understanding the physics
L000085	of FDs. Very few direct measurements of FDs were available, by balloon
L000086	experiments and space satellites \cite{1961JGR....66.3950M,2018ApJ...853...76M,2021ApJ...920L..43A,2023SoPh..298....9L}.
L000087	The PAMELA experiment studied FDs of protons, helium nuclei, and
L000088	electrons, showing charge-sign dependences of their recovery properties
L000089	\cite{2018ApJ...853...76M}. Further investigation of a sample of proton
L000090	FDs using PAMELA data showed that there are two types of recovery times,
L000091	type I with significant energy dependence and type II without energy
L000092	dependence \cite{2023SoPh..298....9L}. Similarly, ground-based detectors
L000093	have identified two distinct types of recoveries
L000094	\cite{2007AdSpR..40..342J,2008JGRA..113.7102U,2016ApJ...827...13Z},
L000095	whose interpretation remains unclear. Using the daily proton fluxes
L000096	measured by AMS-02 \cite{2021PhRvL.127A1102A}, Wang et al. studied the
L000097	properties of FDs caused by CMEs and CIRs, finding that they do not differ
L000098	much from each other \cite{2023ApJ...950...23W} .
L000099	
L000100	Observations of FDs of the leptonic component are even rarer. Daily fluxes
L000101	of electrons and positrons from May 2011 to November 2021 were published by
L000102	AMS-02 \cite{2023PhRvL.130p1001A,2023PhRvL.131o1002A}, but no detailed
L000103	analysis of the FDs has been carried out. An electron FD was reported by
L000104	PAMELA \cite{2018ApJ...853...76M}, shows a faster recovery than protons and
L000105	helium nuclei below 2 GV. The properties of an FD of cosmic ray electrons and
L000106	positrons (hereafter CREs) were measured by the Dark Matter Particle Explorer
L000107	(DAMPE) with significantly improved statistics and wide energy coverage,
L000108	showing clearly energy-dependent recovery times between 2 and 20 GeV
L000109	\cite{2021ApJ...920L..43A}. Note that the DAMPE detector itself does not
L000110	distinguish electrons from positrons due to the lack of magnetic field, and in
L000111	this work we add electrons and positrons together for the study. The fraction
L000112	of positrons in the sample is a few percents in our interested energy range
L000113	\cite{2013PhRvL.110n1102A}. The decrease and recovery behavior observed by
L000114	DAMPE for this event can be properly accounted for using a diffusion
L000115	barrier model \cite{2018ApJ...860..160L,2021ApJ...920L..43A}, the more clear
L000116	underlying physics of FDs needs further exploration using more events. It is
L000117	an intriguing question whether the recovery times of CRE FDs also experience
L000118	two types of energy dependence as thoses of GCR nuclei.
L000119	
L000120	In this work, we analyze the DAMPE CRE data from January 1, 2016 to
L000121	March 31, 2024 to study the population of FDs. A total of eight large
L000122	FDs are identified, each  with maximum decrease amplitudes exceeding $30\%$ of
L000123	the average fluxes. The decrease and recovery properties of these events will
L000124	be investigated in detail.
L000125	
L000126	
L000127	{\it DAMPE detector.} ---
L000128	The DAMPE is a space detector for the observations of cosmic ray nuclei,
L000129	electrons and positrons, and $\gamma$-ray photons
L000130	\cite{2017APh....95....6C,2025arXiv251105409D}.
L000131	The DAMPE detector is composed of four sub-detectors: a plastic scintillator
L000132	detector (PSD; \cite{2017APh....94....1Y}) on the top for charge measurement,
L000133	a silicon-tungsten tracker-converter (STK; \cite{2016NIMPA.831..378A}) for
L000134	trajectory and charge measurement, a Bismuth-Germanium-Oxide imaging
L000135	calorimeter (BGO; \cite{2012ChPhC..36...71Z}) for energy measurement and
L000136	electron-proton separation, and a neutron detector
L000137	(NUD; \cite{2020RAA....20..153H}) for auxiliary electron-proton separation.
L000138	Serving as the key subdetector, the BGO calorimeter consists of 14 layers,
L000139	each containing 22 bars for a total depth of about $32X_0$ which enables
L000140	$\sim1.5\%$ energy resolution for $\sim10$ GeV CREs \cite{2017APh....95....6C}.
L000141	Different from observing the corona graphs, DAMPE is very suitable for
L000142	measurements of CREs with a relatively large acceptance of $\sim0.3$ m$^2$~sr
L000143	and a high energy resolution. The detector was integrated in a dedicated
L000144	satellite platform, and was launched into a sun-synchronous orbit at an
L000145	altitude of 500 km on December 17, 2015 from the Jiuquan base
L000146	\cite{2017APh....95....6C}.
L000147	
L000148	\begin{figure*}
L000149	\centering
L000150	\includegraphics[width=1.0\textwidth]{Fig1_ShowFit.eps}
L000151	\caption{Time profiles of CRE fluxes in four energy bins measured by DAMPE
L000152	in November, 2021 (blue dots), compared with the DAMPE $T_0$ rate (green
L000153	curves) and OULU NM data (red curves). The errorbars of the DAMPE CRE fluxes
L000154	include both the statistical uncertainties and systematic uncertainties,
L000155	added in quadrature. The 4 panels correspond to 4 different CRE energy bins
L000156	as labelled. Arrows in the top-left panel show the two step decreases
L000157	revealed by the NM data and DAMPE $T_0$ data, and the black dashed line
L000158	shows the arrival time of the interplanetary shock.}
L000159	\label{fig:2021FD}
L000160	\end{figure*}
L000161	
L000162	
L000163	{\it CRE selection and flux calculation.} ---
L000164	The housekeeping system of DAMPE records incident counts of events every 4
L000165	seconds, referred to as $T_0$ counts, to monitor the condition of the data
L000166	acquisition system \cite{2019RAA....19..123Z}. The $T_0$ trigger rate is a
L000167	direct measure of the low-energy cosmic ray intensity, which varies
L000168	from dozens Hz near the equator to tens of thousands Hz at the poles.
L000169	Simulations indicate that $T_0$ triggering occurs when the energy of a particle
L000170	is higher than 100 MeV. FD candidates are selected using the DAMPE $T_0$ rate
L000171	and the OULU NM count rate, both exhibit a rapid decrease plus a relatively
L000172	slow recovery. Specifically, if the DAMPE $T_0$ rate decreases by more than
L000173	10\% and the OULU NM count rate decreases over 3\% within 3 days, the
L000174	corresponding time window is labelled as a possible FD event occurs.
L000175	Then a cross match with the SOHO LASCO CME
L000176	catalog\footnote{https://spase-metadata.org/NASA/Catalog/SOHO/LASCO/CME\_Catalog.html} is further required.
L000177	In total we find 8 candidate FDs according to this procedure. The basic
L000178	information of these 8 FD events can be found in Table~S1 of the
L000179	{\tt Supplemental Material}. For each candidate event, we select data from
L000180	10 days before to 30 days after the starting time for the follow-up analysis.
L000181	CRE candidates are selected following the method described in
L000182	Ref.~\cite{2021ApJ...920L..43A}.
L000183	Data recorded during the passage of the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) region
L000184	are excluded. Both events passing the high-energy trigger (HET) and low-energy
L000185	trigger (LET) \cite{2019RAA....19..123Z} conditions are used.
L000186	The reconstructed particle charge \cite{2019APh...105...31D} is set
L000187	to be $Z\le 1.7$, which rejects $\sim99\%$ of nuclei heavier than protons.
L000188	We further require that the shower maximum is not at the edge of the first
L000189	six BGO layers, and the reconstructed track is required to penetrate the
L000190	first four BGO layers. The pre-selection efficiency is shown in Fig.~S1 of
L000191	the {\tt Supplemental Material}. We can see that the efficiency reaches about
L000192	80\% for energies higher than a few GeV. At low energies the efficiency drops
L000193	quickly, due mainly to the trigger efficiency.
L000194	
L000195	After these pre-selections, the main background for CREs is protons.
L000196	We use a particle identification (PID) parameter, defined as
L000197	${\rm PID} = F(E)[\log(R_{r}) \cdot \sin\theta + \log(R_{l}) \cdot \cos\theta]$
L000198	to distinguish CREs from protons, where $F(E)$ is an energy decoupling
L000199	polynomial, ${\theta}$ is a rotation angle, ${R_{r}}$ and ${R_{l}}$ are
L000200	parameters describing the radial and longitudinal extensions of the shower
L000201	in the calorimeter \cite{2021ApJ...920L..43A}. Fig.~S2 of the
L000202	{\tt Supplemental Material} illustrates the distributions of the PID
L000203	parameter for two energy bins, $3.17-3.44$ GeV and $7.35-8.00$ GeV.
L000204	CREs would typically have ${\rm PID}\leq 2$. To properly estimate the
L000205	proton background, we carry out a fit to the data with Monte Carlo (MC)
L000206	simulation templates of CREs and protons. Since CMEs affect electrons
L000207	and protons differently \cite{2018ApJ...853...76M}, the background is
L000208	estimated independently for each energy and time bin. We find that the
L000209	proton background is about 2\% to 8\% for energies from 2 to 20 GeV, with
L000210	about $15\%$ relative changes (differ case by case) during the FD period.
L000211	
L000212	The CRE flux is calculated as
L000213	\begin{equation}
L000214	    I_{i,j}=\frac{N_{i,j}}{{\Delta} E_{i} A_{i} T_{i,j} \eta_{i}},
L000215	    \label{eq2}
L000216	\end{equation}
L000217	where ${N_{i,j}}$ is the number of selected CREs after the background
L000218	subtraction in the ${i}$th energy bin and ${j}$th time bin, ${T_{i,j}}$
L000219	is the corresponding exposure time, ${\Delta E_{i}}$ is the energy bin
L000220	width, ${A_{i}}$ is the geometric acceptance, and $\eta_i$ is the total
L000221	efficiency. To avoid the shielding effect from the geomagnetic field,
L000222	we require that the particle's rigidity is higher than 1.2 times
L000223	of the VRC values. Since the VRC value varies with latitude, the rigidity
L000224	threshold results in variations of the exposure time with time and energy
L000225	(see Fig.~S3 of the {\tt Supplemental Material}). On average,
L000226	the effective exposure time is approximately 80\% of the total time for
L000227	energies above 15 GeV, and decreases gradually to about 30\% at 2 GeV.
L000228	
L000229	\begin{figure*}
L000230	\centering
L000231	\includegraphics[width=1.0\textwidth]{Fig2_Amp.eps}
L000232	\caption{The decrease amplitude as a function of energy, for the eight FDs
L000233	observed by DAMPE.}
L000234	\label{fig:amp}
L000235	\end{figure*}
L000236	
L000237	\begin{figure*}
L000238	\centering
L000239	\includegraphics[width=1.0\textwidth]{Fig3_Rec.eps}
L000240	\caption{The recover time as a function of energy, for the eight FD observed
L000241	by DAMPE. The solid line in each panel shows the best-fit power-law result.}
L000242	\label{fig:tau}
L000243	\end{figure*}
L000244	
L000245	Since we focus on the relative change of the CRE fluxes at a time scale of
L000246	about one month, the main systematic uncertainties are the efficiency
L000247	stabilities. The efficiency fluctuation is estimated to be $<0.15\%$ within
L000248	one month after correcting the temperature effect \cite{2019APh...106...18A}.
L000249	It has also been shown that there is a long-term evolution of the trigger
L000250	efficiency due to radiation damage, electronics aging, and gain decrease
L000251	of photomultipliers, which results in a decrease of the HET efficiency by
L000252	about 5\% per year at 2 GeV and smaller with increasing energies
L000253	\cite{2024NIMPA106969815L}. The systematic uncertainties are much smaller
L000254	than the statistical uncertainties, which are about 3\% at 2 GeV and about
L000255	7\% at 20 GeV.
L000256	
L000257	{\it Results of FDs.} ---
L000258	Fig.~\ref{fig:2021FD} shows the measured CRE fluxes with a time resolution
L000259	of 6 hours in 4 energy bins for the FD event in November, 2021. Also shown
L000260	are the NM data from the OULU station (red), and $T_0$ count rate of DAMPE
L000261	(green) for the McIlwain L-values \cite{1994CASSS..10.....W} of $3.8-4.7$
L000262	which roughly corresponds to the VRC value of the OULU NM station.
L000263	The fluxes 20 days prior to the FD are used as reference for normalizations.
L000264	Note that, although the cutoff rigidities of the OULU station and the DAMPE
L000265	$T_0$ events are similar, they represent essentially different particle
L000266	energies since NMs record secondary neutrons produced by cosmic rays with
L000267	much higher energies. This explains the differences of their decrease
L000268	amplitudes.
L000269	
L000270	
L000271	As can be found from Fig.~\ref{fig:2021FD}, the CRE fluxes experience a fast
L000272	decrease at UT 21:00 on November 3, 2021, reach the minimum at UT 21:00 on
L000273	November 4, and gradually recover to the normal level in about 2 weeks.
L000274	The $T_0$ rate follows a trend similar to that of CRE fluxes. Different from
L000275	the September 2017 event \cite{2021ApJ...920L..43A}, no precursor was observed
L000276	for in this event. The NM profile reaches its minimum at similar time as the
L000277	$T_0$ count rate, but is about 3 hours later than the minimum time of the CRE
L000278	fluxes. The NM profile also shows a faster recovery (with characteristic
L000279	timescale of $\sim2$ days) than the CRE fluxes and the $T_0$ count rate
L000280	(with characteristic timescale of $\sim 4.5$ days).
L000281	Both the NM and the DAMPE $T_0$ data experience two-step decrease features,
L000282	as marked by arrows. Possible explanations of the two-step features could be
L000283	found in Ref.~\cite{2004JGRA..109.2117I}. We note that the $T_0$ rate exhibits
L000284	a larger decrease amplitude in the first step and a smaller amplitude in the
L000285	second step, in contrary to those of NM data. Such differences may again be
L000286	due to different energies. The time profiles for other events can be found
L000287	in Fig.~S6 of the {\tt Supplemental Material}.
L000288	
L000289	The recovery phase of the FD is important in revealing the properties of the
L000290	interplanetary environment disturbed by the CME. The following function is
L000291	employed to fit the recovery profile of an FD:
L000292	\begin{equation}
L000293	\frac{I_{t}}{I_{0}}=1-A_{e} \exp\left(-\frac{t-t_{m}}{\tau}\right),
L000294	    \label{eq3}
L000295	\end{equation}
L000296	where ${I_{t}}$ is the measured CRE flux at time $t$, ${I_{0}}$ is the
L000297	normalization flux before the FD, ${A_{e}}$ is the decrease amplitude,
L000298	${t_{m}}$ is the time of minimum, and ${\tau}$ is the characteristic recovery
L000299	time.
L000300	
L000301	The derived decrease amplitudes and recovery times, for each energy
L000302	bin, are shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:amp} and Fig.~\ref{fig:tau}.

L000304	are conservatively included via a quadratic sum with the statistical
L000305	uncertainties. The decrease amplitude becomes smaller with the increasing
L000306	energy. This can be explained by the fact that particles with
L000307	higher energy are less affected by the magnetic turbulence.
L000308	The energy dependence of the recovery time, however, shows diverse
L000309	properties. For some events, the recovery time becomes shorter with the
L000310	increase of energy (e.g., the 2017-09 event), while for others it remains
L000311	nearly constant for all energies (e.g., the 2017-07 event). These diverse
L000312	behaviors may be related with properties of CMEs causing the FDs. We further
L000313	fit the energy dependence of the recovery time with a power-law function,
L000314	$\tau=aE^b$, and derive the power-law index $b$ for each event. The results
L000315	of the parameter $b$ for the 8 events are shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:tau_VOmega}.

L000318	Fig.~\ref{fig:tau_VOmega} the possible relation between $b$ and a combined
L000319	parameter, $V_{\rm CME}\cdot\Omega$, for these events. The CME velocity
L000320	$V_{\rm CME}$ reflects the strength of the disturbance, and $\Omega$ is the
L000321	solid angle of the CME which reflects the spatial size affected by the CME.
L000322	The CME parameters are extracted from the Wang-Sheeley-Arge (WSA)-Enlil solar
L000323	wind prediction
L000324	model\footnote{https://www.swpc.noaa.gov/products/wsa-enlil-solar-wind-prediction}

L000327	($\Omega$) in a region of 5 to 20 solar radii using corona graphs from three
L000328	different satellites, including STEREO-B COR2, STEREO-A COR2, and LASCO C2.

L000330	important parameter affecting the FDs of GCRs is the ejection direction of
L000331	the CME \cite{2016ApJ...827...13Z}. We classify the CMEs into
L000332	head-on events (I), glancing events (III), and intermediate events (II)

L000339	relationship between $b$ and $V_{\rm CME}\cdot\Omega$ is not clear yet.

L000361	The transport of a charged particle in the heliosphere can be described by
L000362	the Parker's equation \cite{1965P&SS...13....9P} (see the {\tt Supplemental
L000363	Material}). CMEs and other solar activities may disturb the interplanetary
L000364	space, leading to perturbation of the propagation of GCRs. This process can
L000365	be modeled by a fast-moving diffusion barrier \cite{2018ApJ...860..160L}.
L000366	More details about the setting of the diffusion barrier can be found in
L000367	the {\tt Supplemental Material}. We adopt the stochastic differential
L000368	equation (SDE) method to solve Parker's equation with the disturbance by
L000369	CMEs \cite{1999ApJ...513..409Z,2011ApJ...735...83S}. In the modeling, the
L000370	basic parameters of the CMEs, such as the velocity, angular extension, and
L000371	direction, are from the WSA-ENLIL model. The other parameter is the diffusion
L000372	coefficient inside the barrier, which is adjusted to fit the measurements.
L000373	As shown in Fig.~S6 of the {\tt Supplemental Material}, the time
L000374	profiles of the CRE fluxes around the FDs can be reproduced by this model.
L000375	The comparison of the energy-dependence slope parameter $b$ of the recovery
L000376	time between DAMPE observations and simulations is given in Fig.~S7
L000377	of the {\tt Supplemental Material}, which also shows a good consistency.
L000378	The simulation indicates that the recovery behaviors of FDs depend on multiple
L000379	factors, including the motion and geometry of the disturbed regions. Thus the
L000380	diverse properties of the CRE FDs observed by DAMPE reflect the complicated
L000381	propagation processes of particles in the interplanetary space. Note further
L000382	that, the FD events reported in this analysis occurred between 2017 and 2024,
L000383	during which the solar magnetic polarity was always
L000384	positive\footnote{A positive solar magnetic polarity corresponds to an
L000385	outward-pointing heliospheric magnetic field in the Sun's northern hemisphere
L000386	and an inward-pointing magnetic field in the southern hemisphere.} ($A>0$).
L000387	We have a consistent drift direction configuration for all events,
L000388	isolating the additional complexity due to the polarity reversal.
L000389	
L000390	
L000391	{\it Conclusion.} ---
L000392	In this work we study the FDs of CREs recorded by DAMPE, from January, 2016
L000393	to March, 2024. Different from most of existing studies which focus
L000394	on the nuclear component of GCR FDs, this is the first systematic investigation
L000395	of FDs of the electron and positron component. In the total 8 FD events
L000396	detected, the largest decrease amplitude reaches about 30\%. The energy
L000397	dependence of the decrease amplitude and recovery time, from 2 GeV to 20 GeV,
L000398	is well measured. We find that the energy dependence of the recovery time show
L000399	diverse behaviors, which span from strongly energy-dependent to nearly
L000400	energy-independent. Our results further suggest that this diversity is likely
L000401	due to a combined effect of the CME velocity, angular extension, and
L000402	propagation direction. Depending on the ejection direction of the CME
L000403	relative to the Earth, an anti-correlation between the energy dependence
L000404	slope of the recovery time and the velocity times solid angle of the CME
L000405	is revealed by the data. Utilizing a diffusion barrier model, we can
L000406	account for the measurements under the framework of Parker's transport
L000407	equation, based on observed parameters of the CMEs.
L000408	
L000409	With the sunspot number approaching its maximum during the solar cycle 25,
L000410	more FD events are expected to be detected, which will be very helpful in
L000411	testing the phenomenae found in this study. Particularly, additional events
L000412	belonging to with classes II and III will be especially important.
L000413	Furthermore, the comparative studies of FDs of CREs and protons or other
L000414	nuclei, as in Ref.~\cite{2018ApJ...853...76M} but with a significantly
L000415	enlarged sample are of great interest and will be carried out in future works.
L000416	Finally, the joint analysis of the FD events and the sun shadow by groundbased
L000417	cosmic ray experiments \cite{2024Innov...500695} will be crucial in improving
L000418	our understanding of impacts of solar activities on the interplanetary
L000419	magnetic environment and the particle propagation in the heliosphere.

L000575	\section{Electron transport in the heliosphere}
L000576	
L000577	The transport of particles in the heliosphere is described by the Parker's
L000578	equation \cite{1965P&SS...13....9P}:
L000579	\begin{equation}
L000580	    \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = -({\vec{V}}_{\rm sw}
L000581	    + \langle{\vec{V}}_{\rm d}\rangle)\cdot\bigtriangledown{f}
L000582	    + \bigtriangledown\cdot(K^{(\rm s)}\cdot\bigtriangledown{f})
L000583	    + \frac{1}{3}(\bigtriangledown\cdot{\vec{V}}_{\rm sw})
L000584	      \frac{\partial{f}}{\partial{\ln p}},
L000585	    \label{eq5}
L000586	\end{equation}
L000587	where $f(\vec{r},p,t)$ is the particle distribution function, $p$ is momentum,
L000588	${\vec{V}_{\rm sw}}$ is the latitude-dependent solar wind speed,
L000589	$\langle{\vec{V}}_{\rm d}\rangle$ is the pitch-angle averaged drift velocity
L000590	which has the following form \cite{1977ApJ...213..861J,1989ApJ...339..501B}
L000591	\begin{equation}
L000592	    \langle\vec{V}_{\rm d}\rangle = \frac{pv}{3q}\bigtriangledown\times\frac{\vec{B}}{B^{2}},
L000593	    \label{appeq2}
L000594	\end{equation}
L000595	where $q$ and $v$ are charge and velocity of GCR particles, and $\vec{B}$
L000596	is the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF). The variable $K^{(\rm s)}$ is the
L000597	symmetric diffusion tensor, aligned in the IMF coordinate, whose diagonal
L000598	components are the parallel diffusion coefficient $K_{||}$, and the
L000599	perpendicular diffusion coefficiens $K_{\bot\theta}$ and $K_{\bot{r}}$.
L000600

L000603	\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{FigS4_AMSFit.eps}
L000604	\caption{Simulation of the solar modulation effect on electrons, compared
L000605	with the AMS-02 daily electron fluxes \cite{2023PhRvL.130p1001A}, for Bartel
L000606	rotations from 2509 to 2512 in 2017.}
L000607	\label{fig:SM}
L000608	\end{figure*}
L000609	
L000610	\begin{figure*}[!htb]
L000611	\centering
L000612	\includegraphics[width=0.55\linewidth]{FigS5_CME_Location.ps}
L000613	\caption{Schematic plot to show the relative location of the Earth in the CME

L000617	
L000618	In this work the diffusion coefficients are parameterized as \cite{2019ApJ...878....6L})
L000619	\begin{equation}
L000620	  K_{i}=K_{i0}\beta\frac{B_{0}}{B}\left(\frac{P}{P_{k}}\right)^{a}
L000621	  \left[1+\left(\frac{P}{P_{k}}\right)^{\frac{b-a}{c}}\right]^c,
L000622	  \label{appeq3}
L000623	\end{equation}
L000624	where $i$ represents $||$, $\bot\theta$, or $\bot r$; $\beta$ is the particle
L000625	velocity in speed of light, $B$ is the strength of the IMF, $B_{0} \equiv 1$ nT,
L000626	$K_{i0}$ is the normalization diffusion coefficient varying with time, $p_{k}$
L000627	is the break momentum of the diffusion coefficient, $a$, $b$ are the power-law
L000628	indices before and after the break, and $c$ characterizes the smoothness of the
L000629	break.
L000630	
L000631	The IMF is described by the standard Parker field as
L000632	\begin{equation}
L000633	    \vec{B}(r,\theta) = \frac{AB_{\oplus}}{r^{2}}\left(\hat{e}_{r}-\frac{r\Omega{\sin\theta}}{V_{\rm sw}}\hat{e}_{\theta}\right) [1-2H(\theta-\theta_{\rm cs})],
L000634	    \label{addeq5}
L000635	\end{equation}
L000636	where $B_{\oplus}$ is an average of 13 months magnetic field strength before
L000637	the specific time at 1 AU, $A$ describes the polarity of the IMF, defined as
L000638	$A=\pm{1}/\sqrt{1+(\Omega/V_{\rm sw})^{2}}$, $\theta_{\rm cs}$ determines the
L000639	polar extent of the Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS), and $\Omega$ is the
L000640	angular velocity of the sun.
L000641	
L000642	The Parker's equation is solved numerically with the stochastic differential
L000643	equation (SDE) technique \cite{1999ApJ...513..409Z,2011ApJ...735...83S}. The
L000644	parameters of the diffusion coefficient are derived through fitting the
L000645	electron fluxes measured by AMS-02 \cite{2023PhRvL.130p1001A}, using the local
L000646	interstellar spectrum of electrons derived in Ref.~\cite{2021APh...12402495Z}
L000647	(see Fig.~\ref{fig:SM} for an example of the model fitting results in 2017).
L000648	The relatively small portion of positrons has been omitted in the calculation.

L000650	\section{The diffusion barrier model of FD}
L000651	The CME is described by a three dimensional diffusion barrier, in which the
L000652	diffusion coefficient is smaller than the interplanetary value
L000653	\cite{2018ApJ...860..160L}. The diffusion coefficient inside the barrier is
L000654	written as
L000655	\begin{equation}
L000656	    K{'}_{i}=\frac{K_{i}}{1+\rho{h(\theta)f(r)g(\phi)}},
L000657	\end{equation}
L000658	where $\rho$ is the reduction factor, $h(\theta), g(\phi)$, and
L000659	$f(r)$ describes the geometry of the diffusion barrier, as
L000660	\begin{equation}
L000661	    h(\theta)=e^{-\left(\frac{\theta-\theta_{0}}{\theta_{\rm br}}\right)^{10}},
L000662	\end{equation}
L000663	\begin{equation}
L000664	    g(\phi)=e^{-\left(\frac{\phi-\phi_{0}}{\phi_{\rm br}}\right)^{10}},
L000665	\end{equation}
L000666	\begin{equation}
L000667	 f(r)=\left\{
L000668	 \begin{aligned}
L000669	 1-\frac{r-r_{\rm cen}}{r_{a}}&,&r_{\rm cen}<r<r_{\rm fr} \\
L000670	 \frac{r-r_{\rm end}}{r_b}&,& r_{\rm end}<r\leq{r_{\rm cen}}\\
L000671	 0& ,& {\rm others}
L000672	 \end{aligned}
L000673	 \right.,
L000674	\end{equation}
L000675	where $(\theta_0,\phi_0)$ are the direction of the CME center.
L000676	For $\theta_0=\pi/2$ and $\phi_0=0$, the CME hits the Earth head on.
L000677	Parameter $\theta_{\rm br}$ and $\phi_{\rm br}$ describes the extension
L000678	of the barrier. The radical location of the front, center, and end of the
L000679	CME are depicted as $r_{\rm fr}$, $r_{\rm cen}$, and $r_{\rm end}$, and
L000680	the widths of the leading and trailing parts of the barrier are
L000681	$r_{a}=r_{\rm fr}-r_{\rm cen}$ and $r_{b}=r_{\rm cen}-r_{\rm end}$.
L000682	The same SDE method is employed to calculate the time-dependent electron
L000683	fluxes including the diffusion barrier. The parameters used to fit the
L000684	DAMPE data are given in Table \ref{tab:8FD}. A comparison between the
L000685	observed time profiles and simulated ones for the 8 FDs is shown in
L000686	Fig.~\ref{fig:simu}. We also fit the slopes of the energy-dependence of
L000687	the recovery time for the simulation results, which are shown in
L000688	Fig.~\ref{fig:b} with a comparison with observations. Here the
L000689	uncertainties of $b_{\rm Simu}$ are obtained through scaling down
L000690	the simulation sample to similar event statistics with the flight
L000691	data, which makes the comparison between the observations and
L000692	simulations more direct.
